vignette:
He is 55, a Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life in uniform. By the time he becomes a Navy officer, he already understands discipline, hierarchy, and danger as part of ordinary life. What he does not expect is that the experience that stays with him most intensely will come from a period when he is not a combatant at all, but a civilian trapped in a war zone years earlier, before his naval career fully takes shape.

He grows up in a coastal city where military presence is familiar and political violence always seems near enough to be discussed in lowered voices. In his late teens, he is visiting relatives in a neighboring region when fighting erupts suddenly around the city. At first, he and his family tell themselves it will pass in a few days. Instead, roads close, communications become unreliable, and the neighborhood changes almost overnight. Shops shutter. Windows are taped. People begin sleeping in clothes they can run in.

He remembers the sounds first: artillery in the distance, then closer, then so close that the walls tremble before the noise fully lands. He remembers trying to appear calm for his younger cousins while counting seconds between blasts, as if that might tell him whether they were safe. One afternoon, while he and an uncle go out to look for water and bread, they are caught in shelling on a main road. He drops to the ground beside a damaged bus, his face pressed into hot pavement, the air thick with dust and something metallic. A man across the street is hit. He can still recall the stunned expression on the man's face before he collapses. His uncle pulls him by the shirt collar into a doorway, both of them shaking and unable to speak. For the next several weeks, survival narrows into a routine of hiding, rationing food, and listening for whether footsteps outside mean neighbors, soldiers, or something worse.

He sees bodies in the street more than once. He sees a family's apartment burning while no one can reach them. At night he lies awake waiting for the next explosion, his heart already pounding before anything happens. He learns to scan every corner, every roofline, every passing vehicle. He tells himself that fear is useful, that it keeps him alive.

Eventually he gets out. The war moves elsewhere, and life around him begins to reorganize itself with unsettling speed. Other people seem eager to speak about rebuilding, opportunities, the future. He does the same. He does not tell many people how often he dreams of the bus, the road, the body dropping. Instead, he leans harder into structure. The Navy makes sense to him: rules, clear roles, preparedness. Colleagues describe him as composed, exacting, and exceptionally calm under pressure. He builds a career on anticipating threats before others notice them. It looks like talent, and in many ways it is. But he also cannot stop scanning exits, tracking sounds, and feeling a rush of alarm when plans change unexpectedly.

Now, decades later, he is in a relationship with a woman he cares for deeply, but she lives with parts of him that never fully came back from that city. He sleeps lightly and often wakes before dawn, already tense, sometimes drenched in sweat after dreams he struggles to explain. In the dream he is back on the pavement, unable to move, certain that if he lifts his head he will die. On some mornings he sits at the edge of the bed for several minutes, disoriented and irritable, before he can remind himself where he is.

Certain sounds undo him immediately. Fireworks send a shock through his body before he can think. A car backfiring makes him duck and scan. News footage of bombed neighborhoods leaves him cold and nauseated, yet he cannot stop watching. He feels pulled toward images of destruction and then angry with himself afterward. His partner has learned that crowded street festivals, protests, or unfamiliar urban neighborhoods can make him abruptly withdrawn. He studies rooftops, windows, unattended bags. If she asks what is wrong, he says, "Nothing, just paying attention," in a tone that ends the conversation.

He does not think of himself as frightened. He thinks of himself as prepared. Yet the cost shows in quieter moments. He avoids talking about that period because once he starts, his chest tightens and he feels as if he is back there, young and helpless and responsible for keeping everyone alive. He carries a persistent guilt that he survived when others did not, including people whose names he never knew. He can be warm and loyal, but emotionally he often keeps one hand on the door. When his partner reaches for him after he startles awake, he sometimes recoils before recognizing her touch.

At work, he remains highly respected, though colleagues notice he is harsher than he used to be. He has little patience for complacency. Minor mistakes feel to him like openings through which catastrophe enters. He knows his reactions can seem excessive, but inside he experiences the world as a place where disaster is always only seconds away. Even on calm days, he feels his body braced against an impact that never fully comes.
